keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'In 1264, the feudal reign over Tibet was given to Drogön Chögyal Phagpa by Kublai Khan' (Sakya page); Tibet was managed by the Bureau [of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs], separate from the ordinary Yuan provinces under a 'diarchic structure' with the Sakya lama holding nominal religious and political authority while Mongol power dominated (Tibet under Yuan rule page). No area on either page; the Ü-Tsang shape follows the Tibet dossier. The Cliopatria Yuan Dynasty row covers Tibet in 1294-1362 and should be read as the suzerain's shape.

ledger.note: 1264: Kublai Khan gives Phagpa the rule of Tibet. 'In 1264, the feudal reign over Tibet was given to Drogön Chögyal Phagpa by Kublai Khan, founder of the Yuan dynasty.' The Tibet under Yuan rule page dates Sakya Pandita's power to 1244, Phagpa's State Preceptor title to 1260 and the Bureau (Zongzhi Yuan) to 1264; the page names Tibet, the shape Ü-Tsang is a reading.

region.text: Mangyül Gungthang, the south-west Tibetan kingdom with its capital at Dzongkar (a circle of 90 km round Gyirong within the Tibet Autonomous Region, as in the Tibet dossier)

ledger.note: c. 1265: Mangyül Gungthang is founded under Sakya overlordship. The infobox of its page: Tibetan kingdom under Sakya overlordship, one of the thirteen myriarchies, ruled by a Sakya lama viceroy appointed by the Yuan court; Established c. 1265. Drawn as a vassal tint until the Sakya regime ends.

ledger.note: 1285: the Drikung Kagyu rise against the Sakya. The Drikung Kagyu revolted in 1285 with help from Duwa of the Chagatai Khanate.

region.text: Drigung (Drikung) Monastery and its valley, north-east of Lhasa

ledger.note: 1290: the Drikung revolt is crushed. In 1290, Temür Buqa's Yuan army and the Sakyas suppressed it, burning Drigung Monastery and killing about 10,000 people.

wars.outcome: The Yuan army under Temür Buqa and the Sakyas suppress the Drikung Kagyu revolt in 1290: Drigung Monastery is burned and about 10,000 are killed. Duwa of the Chagatai Khanate had backed the rebels.

wars.name: Mongol campaigns in Tibet
wars.outcome: A 1268 expedition under Manggudai and a 1275 campaign by Aurughchi; by 1280 Mongol rule was considered secure. The Yuan's own campaigns; no change of the Sakya shape.

notes: Written for ea-06-x at the request of the ea-06-b report (counterpart sakya-regime, Sakya regime under the Yuan, 1354-1358), widened to the whole Sakya period 1264-1358 because the Tibet under Yuan rule page dates the regime from the 1264 grant. Cliopatria has no row (its Yuan Dynasty row covers the years). Pages: Tibet under Yuan rule, Sakya, Phagmodrupa dynasty. Disagreements: the Tibet under Yuan rule infobox ends Yuan rule over Tibet in 1354, its text dates the end of Sakya lama succession to 1358; the Phagmodrupa page gives 1354-1358 for the supersession; the Sakya page does not cover 1244, 1260 or 1358; the infobox capital Drigung Gompa (1240-1264) is not explained by the text and is not used. Relation to the Yuan: the Sakya lamas ruled as the Yuan's viceregal government (the dpon-chen was confirmed by the emperor at Dadu, and Yuan military posts and a Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs stood over them). That suzerainty belongs in the Yuan dossier (ea-06-a) as a vassal_start/vassal_end with counterpart sakya-regime; this dossier cannot carry it. The tibet dossier's 1354 and 1358 events name yuan-dynasty as counterpart and should name sakya-regime. Not on any page: the Sakya shape beyond Ü-Tsang (Ngari, the thirteen myriarchies are not mentioned), a ruler list (the Sakya page only says the Khön family leads the school; Phagpa was Imperial Preceptor 1270-1274 by the Yuan list), and the year Sakya Pandita's grant became a territory. Mangyül Gungthang, the Sakya vassal kingdom of the south-west (c. 1265-1619), is recorded as a vassal here and has its own dossier (mangyul-gungthang, this batch). Counterparts needing dossiers: Drikung Kagyu (the Drikung lordship, 1285-1290), yuan-dynasty (ea-06-a), tibet (ea-06-b, exists).
